body: Sounds very great, could you explain how it would interact with double/triple buffering? Because it feels like turning off/on this exact feature.

By double/triple buffering, do you mean the frame queue, or the swapchain? When enabled, this effectively forces a single-buffered frame queue, as if you set `frame_queue_size` to 1, but without actually using a smaller frame queue (size remains the same, just doesn't get filled). Right now there's no way to set `frame_queue_size` to 1 without modifying the engine, so with this change you can bring the latency one frame lower than you could otherwise.

The swapchain is unaffected, so if you want the lowest latency with standard (FIFO) V-Sync you'll need to set `swapchain_image_count` to 2.

> ### Feedback
> * Should we use low-latency mode in the editor automatically? I think we can make it always be used in the 2D editor, script editor and AssetLib tabs. In the 3D editor, it would be enabled whenever the 3D editor viewport doesn't have focus (i.e. the mouse cursor isn't on the 3D editor viewport). This would avoid skewing performance measurements with the **View Frame Time** panel.
>   
>   * There could be an editor setting to override this behavior, with the values **Auto** (default), **Never**, **Always**.

I don't see much use case for having this in the editor, unless there's some weird crossover caused by the new game embedding feature.

Worth noting that the low latency gains here diminish significantly once you go beyond 120hz - this mode is primarily intended for 2D or lightweight 3D games running on 60hz displays. Also worth noting that nVidia Reflex and AMD Anti-Lag have driver-level knowledge that could minimize the FPS impact (since they're aware of the current CPU/GPU timings and can optimize for that), but this PR is at least a start.

> I don't see much use case for having this in the editor, unless there's some weird crossover caused by the new game embedding feature.

We have a lot of issues related to input lag in the editor, such as https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/71795.

Disabling V-Sync avoids these issues, but it introduces tearing (which is mostly an issue for the 2D/3D viewports – probably not much of a problem in the script editor where scrolling is mostly vertical). Also, regardless of V-sync, we can get further improvements to latency by reducing frame queuing.

In general, non-game applications are the area where I'd expect the low-latency mode to be most useful – and the Godot editor is a non-game application made with Godot :slightly_smiling_face:
Discussed with @Calinou and we'll probably handle low latency in the editor in a followup PR.

> Interestingly, I have consistently found that Compatibility has one extra frame of latency in fullscreen mode compared to windowed mode, even in 4.4rc1. Maybe I'll open an inssue for this...

This is driver behavior, I'm pretty sure. OpenGL lets drivers do additional frame queueing if they want, but are expected to flush that queue when `glFinish` is called (which this PR does with low latency mode active). Could also change the number of queued/pre-rendered frames in the driver settings. The driver-level low-latency setting might also work.

Driver settings won't have any effect in D3D12 or Vulkan though. With those APIs, frame queueing is handled by the client application, so the only way to disable that queueing is with this PR.

I am not certain it makes sense to include this in Godot at all, but if it is included, these are some changes that I think are needed to make it less of a foot-gun. The current setting name and descriptions sound like the sort of thing that may be presented to a player, rather than a game developer.

To make the setting more useful to game developers, I think the setting should be called something like "CPU Blocking" with these options:
- Do not block
- Block CPU processing

The description could say something like:
- "Block CPU processing" causes the CPU to wait until GPU processing is finished before continuing to process the next frame. This may result in low framerates and stutters, but can reduce output latency. This setting should not be enabled by default, but can be presented to the user as an option to favor lower latency instead of higher framerates.

Additionally, it should disable/grey out the "Frame Queue Size" setting and should only be visible when "Advanced Settings" are shown. I also think it should be placed near the V-Sync settings in Rendering Device instead of in its own section.

...Also, how does this behave when the frame queue size is higher than 2? I expect that it makes no sense to have this as an option at all when frame queue size is higher than 2?

All that said, I really don't know if this is something that should be included in Godot at all, because disabling V-Sync sounds like a much more reasonable and safer option to me. I understand disabling V-Sync results in screen tearing, but I suspect that players who want lower latency and are using a 60 Hz display without VRR are also the sorts of players who don't have the CPU headroom to enable this setting.

> All that said, I really don't know if this is something that should be included in Godot at all, because disabling V-Sync sounds like a much more reasonable and safer option to me. I understand disabling V-Sync results in screen tearing, but I suspect that players who want lower latency and are using a 60 Hz display without VRR are also the sorts of players who don't have the CPU headroom to enable this setting.

As I understand it, this PR also helps with V-Sync off latency at an identical framerate, although I haven't tested this. Not to mention that in VRR scenarios, you'll want to have V-Sync enabled and a FPS cap slightly lower than the monitor refresh rate.

> I am not certain it makes sense to include this in Godot at all, but if it is included, these are some changes that I think are needed to make it less of a foot-gun. The current setting name and descriptions sound like the sort of thing that may be presented to a player, rather than a game developer.

The "low latency" nomenclature is in line with tech like nVidia Reflex and AMD Anti-Lag.

> To make the setting more useful to game developers, I think the setting should be called something like "CPU Blocking" with these options:
> 
> * Do not block
> * Block CPU processing
> 
> The description could say something like:
> 
> * "Block CPU processing" causes the CPU to wait until GPU processing is finished before continuing to process the next frame. This may result in low framerates and stutters, but can reduce output latency. This setting should not be enabled by default, but can be presented to the user as an option to favor lower latency instead of higher framerates.

"Block CPU processing" as a name doesn't really communicate the intent of the mode, and is also rather vague (block CPU when? For what?). Also, we probably don't want a setting named something this low level if at some point we want to integrate different implementations of low-latency.

> Additionally, it should disable/grey out the "Frame Queue Size" setting and should only be visible when "Advanced Settings" are shown. I also think it should be placed near the V-Sync settings in Rendering Device instead of in its own section.

"Frame Queue Size" should still be adjustable, because low latency mode can be changed at runtime. "Rendering Device" refers to the Mobile/Forward+ renderers that use Vulkan/D3D12, and as a subsystem does not apply to Compatibility/OpenGL. I want to make low latency mode available for all renderers.

> ...Also, how does this behave when the frame queue size is higher than 2? I expect that it makes no sense to have this as an option at all when frame queue size is higher than 2?

Low latency mode will functionally act the same regardless of the frame queue size. All it does is flush the frame queue. The swapchain size, on the other hand, does have a noticeable impact with this enabled.

> All that said, I really don't know if this is something that should be included in Godot at all, because disabling V-Sync sounds like a much more reasonable and safer option to me. I understand disabling V-Sync results in screen tearing

Tearing at 60hz looks dreadful and is easily avoided. The Linux world has spent many, many years dealing with users agonizing over tearing in their applications, to the point that many configurations don't even allow you to disable the global V-Sync. So disabling it isn't really an option here.

> but I suspect that players who want lower latency and are using a 60 Hz display without VRR are also the sorts of players who don't have the CPU headroom to enable this setting.

The entire reason I wanted to introduce this option in the first place is because not everyone has a 240hz VRR monitor. And even then, chances are the hardware can run my projects at a full 60 FPS even without pipelining. Again, my games are generally retro-style 2D pixel art, running at 640x480 resolution (or lower). That may have been a problem for GPUs back in the Windows XP days with GeForce FX cards, but today, if your GPU can handle OpenGL 3, chances are it can run the game at full speed and doesn't need to make use of CPU/GPU parallelism. I've seen firsthand that even integrated laptop GPUs from ~7 years ago can handle hundreds of layers of 2D graphics at 60 FPS.

All I want is to be able to turn off this additional latency that won't benefit my games. In terms of user feedback, I get complaints about OpenGL driver bugs, antivirus false positives, and control issues, but never anything about performance.

I would also like to reiterate that frame queueing for D3D12/Vulkan cannot be disabled by the user through driver settings. Making this frame queueing optional in the engine is also going to be required for nVidia Reflex and AMD Anti-Lag going forward. It's also important for VR, where you want your head and hand tracking to be as closely synced to your real movements as possible.

V-Sync is also forced on Android/iOS/Web platforms with no way for projects to disable it, so this is another area where having low-latency OpenGL rendering matters (e.g. for drawing apps that use tablet input).

Ok, thanks for the comments!

The one thing I still think needs improvement is the "low latency mode" setting name. I understand this is similar nomenclature to other player-facing features, but it is overly opaque to a game developer who wants to know what sort of change it makes to engine behaviour. Maybe my suggestion of "CPU Blocking" is problematic, but there has to be something else that better describes what engine behaviour changes when this feature is enabled...

Maybe something along the lines of "CPU/GPU Pipelining"? The forward slash wouldn't work, but I think it'd better describe what's going on under the hood. The "pipeline" term matches with the current Android swappy options in Godot:

![2025-02-27 18_07_15-Greenshot](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1f080df3-a8fa-47dc-a466-ddc4b64f0b36)

...Though it would have been nice to have the Android settings implemented in a less silo'd-off way. I do want to leave the door open to the possibility of multiple "low latency" backends for different hardware configurations. So the basic frame queue flushing would be one such backend, with the ability to introduce others further down the road. I just didn't want to put the cart before the horse.

I don’t think it’s a good idea to overload the setting with behaviours that are very different based on the platform, and I do think it is a good idea to share the setting between OpenGl and Vulkan, like this PR implements, because essentially the same behaviour can be done with both rendering methods.

Why shouldn’t low latency be default?

> Why shouldn’t low latency be default?

This is exactly the reason that I strongly believe calling this "low latency mode" is highly problematic 😂. This is not low latency mode, it is an option to disable concurrent GPU and CPU processing, which greatly reduces the time available for GPU and CPU processing, while also reducing latency :)

My argument for forcing on concurrent GPU and CPU processing is if we don't the game developers and engine contributors will get used to concurrency off.

I would prefer reducing latency but forcing off concurrency is a bad thing.

> My argument for forcing on concurrent GPU and CPU processing is if we don't the game developers and engine contributors will get used to concurrency off.

The PR defaults to concurrent processing being enabled (`low_latency_mode` set to `RENDER_LATENCY_PRIORITIZE_FRAMERATE`), and since it's a project setting, it should be easy enough to troubleshoot by looking at the user's project in question.

> I would prefer reducing latency but forcing off concurrency is a bad thing.

This is a source of latency that cannot be removed without removing the concurrency. The concurrency in question is great in scenarios where we want to keep the GPU busy with work. But if the application is only taking 2 ms to render a frame and we're targeting 60 FPS with V-Sync (16.67 ms), all we're doing is delaying those frames. In this scenario, we gain nothing from the concurrency, yet we end up with 33 ms of added latency. There is more to the user experience than just raw graphical throughput. Latency matters, too. This is why I object to concurrency being forced on at all times.

> This is exactly the reason that I strongly believe calling this "low latency mode" is highly problematic 😂. This is not low latency mode, it is an option to disable concurrent GPU and CPU processing, which greatly reduces the time available for GPU and CPU processing, while also reducing latency :)

Fair enough. I'll go ahead and adjust the naming to better reflect what's going on. I wanted this to be an extensible mode with multiple backends, but perhaps it's too high level and potentially misleading that way.

> I wanted this to be an extensible mode with multiple backends, but perhaps it's too high level and potentially misleading that way.

I get where you're coming from, especially with the Android modes you mentioned, and I could see that this was your thought process based on the main PR text, but for the reasons discussed, keeping the setting simple, focused, and descriptive will be best overall I think.

Additionally, as I see it, the Android style auto-magical modes could be tricky to implement "flawlessly"... But with the nothing more than what is currently implemented in this PR, a developer could render a few frames of a complex representative scene behind a black fill to benchmark the host and adjust this setting based on the results. Then the game could monitor performance stats to adjust later if needed.

In fact, all of this sort of auto-magical implementation could be implemented as a plugin. I definitely like keeping the engine as lean as possible, so this plugin approach for automatic runtime tuning of this setting sounds more attractive to me than a built-in feature that might have a number of caveats or edge case scenarios where it introduces hitches or stutters.

Just updated the PR. Ready for review again.

Changelog:

- Renamed "low latency mode" to "CPU/GPU synchronization mode", including functions, enums, ProjectSetting, and CLI switch.
- Moved ProjectSetting from `rendering/latency/low_latency_mode` to `rendering/driver/synchronization/cpu_gpu_sync`.
- Hid the ProjectSetting behind Advanced Settings.
- Replaced `glFinish` with `glFenceSync` + `glClientWaitSync` as this is the modern way to do things in GL.
- Small wording tweaks in enums for easier reading.
- Fixed merge conflicts.

> In this scenario, which of these two settings (prefer high framerate or prefer low latency) results in lower input latency?

The 60 FPS game with Prefer High Framerate should have lower overall latency in this scenario (and pixel response times will be better on the display, as each frame will be displayed for less time).

> In this scenario, which of these two settings (prefer high framerate or prefer low latency) results in lower input latency?

According to the [V-Sync Simulator](https://darksylinc.github.io/vsync_simulator/), the lower latency mode will have less lag even at 30 FPS, but only in GPU-limited scenarios. Otherwise latency remains around the same (but with more deviation, and worst case latency is sometimes worse). So the answer is "it depends, but lower latency mode will *probably* still have lower latency in general".

> > In this scenario, which of these two settings (prefer high framerate or prefer low latency) results in lower input latency?
> 
> The 60 FPS game with Prefer High Framerate should have lower overall latency in this scenario (and pixel response times will be better on the display).

For this reason, I believe that the setting names of "Prefer High Framerate" and "Prefer Low Latency" are misleading and should be renamed to something that describes the technical behaviour. Importantly, the current "Prefer Low Latency" mode might not actually produce lower latency in all scenarios, so its documentation should only state something like: "This setting will only result in lower latency on devices that have enough processing headroom to achieve framerates that well exceed the native refresh rate."

I don't understand enough of the technical side of this to be certain, but my suggestion is that CPU/GPU Sync setting should have these options:
- Concurrent
- Consecutive

As I was finishing writing my first response, I see that this isn't entirely black-and-white. Regardless, `Concurrent` and `Consecutive` are better setting names to me; the documentation can go into detail regarding how latency may be reduced with `Consecutive` CPU/GPU Sync in some scenarios.

> As I was finishing writing my first response, I see that this isn't entirely black-and-white. Regardless, `Concurrent` and `Consecutive` are better setting names to me; the documentation can go into detail regarding how latency may be reduced with `Consecutive` CPU/GPU Sync in some scenarios.

Yeah, that is why I chose to use the word "Prefer" (previously "Prioritize" but I decided that's too wordy), meaning "we'll attempt to lower latency through forcing synchronization but it's not guaranteed".

If we choose to go with a more technical term, I think we should go with "Parallel" and "Sequential" instead of "Concurrent" and "Consecutive" (both start with C, and are maybe less familiar terms to people).

> If we choose to go with a more technical term, I think we should go with "Parallel" and "Sequential" instead of "Concurrent" and "Consecutive" (both start with C, and are maybe less familiar terms to people).

I would be equally happy with either or both of these terms; I believe they are effectively synonymous to my suggestions in this context!

Our `cpu_gpu_sync_mode` property needs a new home. Back when it was called `low_latency_mode` it lived in `Engine`, next to the FPS limit properties and similar, but now that we're repositioning this as more of an advanced rendering setting, it doesn't make sense to have it there.

I already explained [why disabling V-Sync is not an option](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/100031#issuecomment-2689221160). We need *some* mode that avoids tearing while also providing low latency where appropriate. Having control over pre-rendered frames is also important for VR applications (and you *definitely* don't want screen tearing there).

> If auto mode means "dynamically switch between Parallel and Sequential like Swappy's auto_fps_auto_pipeline", I'm onboard.

Yes. That's what I meant.

> If it means late input reads via sleep,

I also planned on adding this. Your explanation isn't wrong but it skips too many things:

1. Potential frame pacing issues are always unavoidable, even for Auto mode. Ultimately it boils down to a system to decide what's the best strategy to present by predicting the future; and when we're wrong it _will_ result in stutter. All we can do is minimize how often we're wrong (hopefully never). I'll give an extreme example: If Auto keeps deciding to alternate between Sequential and Parallel every frame, we'll get massive stutter. Obviously such behavior is a bug. But the moment Auto decides it's time to switch between Sequential or Parallel, frame pacing will change. And that results in a small micro stutter.
2. For Sleep, you're assuming a very rigid implementation. It wouldn't be implemented so poorly:
    - You assumed the amount of time to sleep would be a fixed value in a config setting. It would **never** be implemented like that. The amount of time to sleep is estimated based on past frame measurements and query of monitor refresh rate.
    - Sleep needs to give an overhead. i.e. if we think the frame will take 2ms to process and render, then we overestimate it to 4ms. How aggressive the overestimation could be tweakable. Past behavior can also help (e.g. by calculating standard deviation).
    - How long to sleep would use a rolling average. Meaning that if we're wrong just once; only a frame of stutter will happen. And if we're always wrong, then there's no stutter (only very high latency) until the rolling average adjusts itself to the right side of the frame (so that we go back to low latency; it would micro-stutter once when we go from being "wrong" to being "right"). Rolling averages give a lot of predictability and smooth behavior.
    - Latency sensitive games (e.g. Guitar Hero-like games) need a calibration phase anyway. Whether using Auto, Sleep or none of the two; because latency depends on CPU power, GPU power, and monitor refresh rate.

How Auto and/or Sleep can go very wrong:
   - Refresh Rate settings queried are wrong. This can happen with multiple monitors setup. It can also happen on Android with dynamic refresh rates. Workaround is to allow end users to override detected refresh rate. This affects both Auto and Sleep solutions.
   - Sleep() is not guaranteed to return immediately. It can be very inaccurate. Possible solutions are to probe how accurate Sleep is. If we detect it's inaccurate, we switch to an empty loop (but that would burn battery) or simply disable sleep-based latency reduction (since it cannot be used reliably and draining battery is not an option).
   - Alt+Tab and similar external events can mess up measurements; so we need a way to detect them and reset the measurements, so we gracefully recover. Failing to do so would cause the auto and sleep algorithms to incorrectly add latency for some time (even minutes) until the massively-displaced rolling average catches up. Putting a cap on rolling average can also help.

> 1. Potential frame pacing issues are always unavoidable, even for Auto mode.

If an "auto" feature is implemented into the core of Godot rather than with an extension/script plugin, it would mean that Godot maintainers would need to attempt to minimize the stutters across all platforms and configurations for the indefinite future. Additionally, they would need to handle additional issues being reported and walk the difficult line of what is a bug and what is an expected behaviour. This is not a load that should be put on the Godot maintainers without careful consideration of the long term impact to Godot maintenance. Implementing it first as an extension sounds like a better approach for this reason. If there are new hooks that need to be exposed, they can be exposed through GDExtension PRs.

And even if the end goal is to implement it into core, a plugin in the asset library would allow the auto approach to be battle tested and refined before committing to an implementation in core.

> 1. Potential frame pacing issues are always unavoidable, even for Auto mode. Ultimately it boils down to a system to decide what's the best strategy to present by predicting the future; and when we're wrong it _will_ result in stutter. All we can do is minimize how often we're wrong (hopefully never). I'll give an extreme example: If Auto keeps deciding to alternate between Sequential and Parallel every frame, we'll get massive stutter. Obviously such behavior is a bug. But the moment Auto decides it's time to switch between Sequential or Parallel, frame pacing will change. And that results in a small micro stutter.

This sounds more like a good case against auto mode (though if the auto mode switch happens the moment a V-Sync is missed, it might not be *too* noticeable).

> 2. For Sleep, you're assuming a very rigid implementation. It wouldn't be implemented so poorly:
>    
>    * You assumed the amount of time to sleep would be a fixed value in a config setting. It would **never** be implemented like that. The amount of time to sleep is estimated based on past frame measurements and query of monitor refresh rate.

I didn't really make that assumption, I just gave a simplified example. And the fact that it'd be automatic implies that it'll try to sleep much more aggressively than just 4ms.

>    * Sleep needs to give an overhead. i.e. if we think the frame will take 2ms to process and render, then we overestimate it to 4ms. How aggressive the overestimation could be tweakable. Past behavior can also help (e.g. by calculating standard deviation).

And this is what I was describing when I said that having to tweak it would be problematic. For a 3D game you especially need to consider frametime variance. [Here's DigitalFoundry illustrating just how much it can fluctuate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0yhacyXcizA) in Monster Hunter: Wilds, a game that's currently got "Mixed" reviews on Steam due to poor optimization. I've seen folks complain about stutters when moving the camera in other games too, such as Yooka-Laylee. For some, stutters like these can cause motion sickness. Adding a dynamic sleep on top of that would probably make these stutter issues worse.

>    * How long to sleep would use a rolling average. Meaning that if we're wrong just once; only a frame of stutter will happen. And if we're always wrong, then there's no stutter (only very high latency) until the rolling average adjusts itself to the right side of the frame (so that we go back to low latency; it would micro-stutter once when we go from being "wrong" to being "right"). Rolling averages give a lot of predictability and smooth behavior.
>    * Latency sensitive games (e.g. Guitar Hero-like games) need a calibration phase anyway. Whether using Auto, Sleep or none of the two; because latency depends on CPU power, GPU power, and monitor refresh rate.

The problem is drift. If you configure the game for an input latency of 60ms and the game suddenly starts delaying the input reads for an additional 10ms, you'll end up missing notes because what used to be perfect timing is now going to be slightly late. And then you start questioning your own calibration, wondering why it didn't work in-game when it seemed fine during calibration, unaware that the timing was being changed due to an implementation detail. This will be complicated further by variations in frametimes due to the 3D camera panning around the venue.

> * Sleep() is not guaranteed to return immediately. It can be very inaccurate. Possible solutions are to probe how accurate Sleep is. If we detect it's inaccurate, we switch to an empty loop (but that would burn battery) or simply disable sleep-based latency reduction (since it cannot be used reliably and draining battery is not an option).

More than that, resource-intensive background processes (like Windows Update) and more generally context switches on modern operating systems mean that a `Sleep()` call may end up returning much later than what the measured accuracy might lead one to believe.

Somewhat related to your mention of an empty loop though, with #99178 the Windows platform now does a conservative `Sleep()` and then does a busy wait for the remaining few milliseconds, and it's been a big improvement to framepacing. Having said that, we're still talking about a multitasking operating system where anything could happen, what with the sleep duration being at the mercy of whatever the OS task scheduler decides to do (to say nothing of hardware interrupts and buggy device drivers).

Personally, I think it'd be more useful to look into waitable swapchains, since that lets us delay frame processing (including input reads) until we know we have a swap image we can use. That would give us a more stable sleep than just guessing how long to wait. It could also fix #100025. Main concern though is platform support.

I agree with darksylinc that, ultimately, we should only have two modes "Auto" and "Parallel". "Sequential" is simply too dangerous to expose to users and in the vast majority of cases it isn't even useful for users. What makes sequential dangerous is that it relies on both the content of the game being simple enough _and_ the users' hardware being powerful enough. Where _enough_ means that the combined cost on GPU and CPU is less than the target frame rate. In order to make use of "sequential", the developer needs to have a good understanding of what the setting means and the tradeoff that they are incurring _and_ the developer needs tight control over their target hardware. In practice, outside of console development, these assumptions are never met. Further, in reality, the first assumption will almost never be met except by a few very skilled developers. Given that "sequential" is a massive footgun, its best not to expose it at all. 

To further explain what I mean, let's look at a few hypotheticals.  

#### Very simple 2D game, specific hardware

This may be the case if you are making a retro arcade game and you are targeting fixed hardware (maybe for a console game, or a specific art display etc.). In this case the "Auto" mode will behave exactly the same as "Sequential". This class of game would benefit from "Auto" being on by default with the option to use parallel in case the user is targeting a high frame rate.

#### Very simple game, any hardware

Most games won't have control over the hardware, this is true for anything released on desktop devices. On Mobile, you have some level of control (can filter out older hardware by excluding older OS versions), but still have a huge range in performance. Due to the uncertainty of the target hardware "sequential" is likely not viable. In some rare cases, it may be viable, but the developer would need to do extensive testing on very low end devices and accept that their game may perform unacceptably slow on some hardware. 

In this case "Auto" or "Parallel" will be the best choices. On most devices "Auto" will function the same as "sequential", but it still allows the low end devices to achieve the highest frame rate and it takes away all the testing required by the developer. Keep in mind, most indie devs don't have the means to test on a wide range of hardware, so an option that requires them to test on dozens of devices across the spectrum of performance is not viable. 

#### Non simple game, specific hardware

If the game is not simple, it can't use "sequential" unless on very powerful hardware. In this case "sequential" could be useful if you are only targeting one specific piece of high end hardware (e.g. a console). But likely "Auto" will be just as useful and will save the developer time. Since the hardware is fixed, "auto" won't add stuttering as it won't turn on and off.

### Non simple game, any hardware

In this case "Auto" may be acceptable (but may create stuttering if the performance of the game is not stable), but "Parallel" is likely the best choice, if only to save the overhead of auto. "Sequential" would be harmful, even if the developer desires better latency. Other low latency tools should be exposed instead. 

I do like @allenwp's idea of leaving the "Auto" mode to plugin developers. But unfortunately, that requires us to expose "sequential" mode to everyone. For the reasons above, I don't think sequential mode should be exposed to everyone and I don't want to expose a setting with a big warning that says "do not use". IMO that is contrary to Godot's philosophy to keep things simple, difficult to break, and easy to understand. That is why I think that we should only expose the "Auto" mode which will give ideal behaviour in most cases and "Parallel" which allow users to disable this behaviour if they want to always favour high performance

> I agree with darksylinc that, ultimately, we should only have two modes "Auto" and "Parallel". "Sequential" is simply too dangerous to expose to users and in the vast majority of cases it isn't even useful for users.

"Sequential" actually has a few advantages over "Auto":

- Profiling: "Auto" will not give consistent results when profiling for performance optimizations. It might switch to "Sequential" for some scenes but not others, or it might constantly toggle back and forth between "Sequential" and "Parallel", or worse, it might run on "Sequential" for some users but not others. I can see this being the cause of subtle, hard-to-debug performance issues, not to mention obscure the developer's ability to troubleshoot existing issues.
- Frame-by-frame debugging: Sometimes it's useful to run a game frame-by-frame to troubleshoot the cause of bugs that can only be observed for a single frame. If in "Parallel" mode, you can't actually see the result of everything that occurred on the next frame, only the frame after (or worse). Only in "Sequential" mode is there a guarantee that this will happen. "Auto" is also likely not going to be suitable here, because simply pausing the game will likely throw it into "Parallel" mode, meaning the next frame advance may suddenly appear to have no visible changes, resulting in confusion.
- VR and framegen: For VR, low latency is paramount. Without it, users can easily get motion sick just by moving their head (which is one of the reasons why so many VR applications target 90 FPS and not 60, as 90 offers lower swapchain latency). The VR compositor uses async reprojection to smooth out the gaps between frames so the view still responds appropriately to the user's head movement. This reprojection only works properly when there's no delay to the frames being rendered. Granted, the fact that this is handled by the compositor improves the situation considerably. But it's apparently enough of an issue that nVidia saw fit to include a "Virtual Reality pre-rendered frames" tweakable in their driver settings, which currently defaults to 1, the lowest value. Framegen is similar to VR reprojection/motion smoothing. In fact, I'm pretty sure that nVidia won't even let you enable their framegen without also enabling nVidia Reflex.
- The need for tuning: My concerns over the dynamic sleep wait extend to "Auto" mode as well. How do we decide when it's okay to switch between "Parallel" and "Sequential"? How can we be sure that the framerate increase from switching to "Parallel" won't cause it to switch back to "Sequential"? Granted we would likely be measuring CPU/GPU execution times instead of simply looking at framerate, but I feel like the mode switch could cause unforeseen knock-on effects. We'd need some sort of threshold to prevent switching back and forth too often. But this might also be affected by the scene's contents, and variations in CPU/GPU load, not just between different games but also drivers and hardware.
- Implicit vs explicit behavior: The trend in the industry lately, both for graphics programming and for programming in general, has been a move away from implicit behavior. The more magical stuff we try to put on top of the implementation to "guess the user's intent" or "protect the user from hurting themself", the more likely we are to introduce subtle, hard-to-debug issues. This is, after all, why Vulkan became a thing. I understand that Vulkan has made writing a custom engine way harder, and is a good reason why we need easier tools to keep game making accessible. On the other hand, Godot aspires to be many things, from an easy-to-use tool for beginners, all the way up to an engine that meets the needs of professionals. After all, this is Godot Engine, not Scratch.
- Plugin API: If we want to support nVidia Reflex, it will have to be through a plugin, as the SDK is locked behind a developer portal that forbids redistribution. And in order to make plugin support, we will need "Sequential" mode. If we tried to run the "Auto" logic at the same time, it would likely result in a mess and fail to work properly. AMD Anti-Lag is open-licensed, but the same thing would apply if it were implemented as a plugin. Using these technologies will likely give better results (better FPS, less stutter) than us trying to roll our own "Auto" mode.
- Latency: Sometimes low latency is more important, even if it's at the expense of framerate. More on that later.

There's also support/maintenance load. Consider the following scenarios:

- User enables "Sequential" mode and notices an FPS drop. They report an issue. We notice that they switched to "Sequential" mode. We point to the documentation, indicate that this is expected behavior, and close the issue.
- User enables "Auto" mode (or it's enabled for them) and notices an FPS drop. They report an issue. Someone else tries their MRP and can't reproduce, because "Auto" mode acts differently on their machine. Reporter insists that they can still reproduce. Someone else looks inside the project. In the case of "Auto" mode being default, nothing looks out of the ordinary in `project.godot`. With nobody able to find the cause, there's a bunch of back-and-forth on "but it works fine in this other scene" "what happens if you change the scene" "it's different but I don't know why" "are your thermals too hot/did you change your CPU governor/are you using the Compatibility renderer" etc, etc, etc, until it becomes a big mess.

Personally, I prefer the one that's easier to diagnose and close.
